<result>## Findings

### 1. `committed_write_pseudonyms` decompresses every committed pseudonym eagerly — the residual Θ(n) term the pin doesn't remove
`/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box/.claude/worktrees/agent-a3ae17b99e0dc6e1b/crates/engine/src/gate/adoption.rs:316-328` (built at `:396`)

**Cost.** `filter_map(Ed25519Verifier::from_bytes)` runs `VerifyingKey::from_bytes` → `CompressedEdwardsY::decompress` for up to `1 + MAX_GRANT_BLOBS` = 1025 keys, on every resolved IPNS record, before a single signature is checked. A decompression is one field-element sqrt (~250 field ops), roughly **8-10% of a full `verify_strict`**. It also materialises `1025 × 192 B ≈ 200 KB` of `VerifyingKey` (dalek 2.x stores compressed bytes *and* the expanded `EdwardsPoint`) plus a 1025-node `BTreeSet` for the dedup — all in a WASM worker's heap.

After this PR at most `1 + (index of the pinned signer)` of those keys are ever touched. The PR's own claim is that worst-case work drops from `pseudonyms × structures` to `pseudonyms + structures`; this line quietly keeps an unconditional `pseudonyms` term that is *independent of how much verifying actually happens*. The sharpest case is the minimal section (owner blob + write body = 2 structures) under a 1024-grantee commitment: **1025 decompressions ≈ 100 verify-equivalents to perform 2 verifies — a ~50× surcharge**. In the common honest case (owner signs, index 0, ~50 grantees, ~10 structures) it is ~5 verify-equivalents on top of 10 real verifies, i.e. ~30-50% overhead on the stage-3 budget.

**Cheaper alternative.** Keep the deduped raw bytes and decompress inside the trial loop, storing the *decompressed* key rather than an index:

```rust
struct StructureAuthenticator {
    committed: Vec<[u8; 32]>,        // 33 KB worst case, not 200 KB
    pinned: Option<Ed25519Verifier>, // holds the key, not an index into `committed`
}
```
The scan then does `Ed25519Verifier::from_bytes(*pk)` immediately before the trial verify it feeds, so decompressions performed == trials performed, and a non-decompressible pseudonym simply never verifies — identical semantics, and the new `a_commitment_naming_no_usable_write_pseudonym_authenticates_nothing` test still passes verbatim (empty `committed` ⇒ no candidate ⇒ same verdict). Storing the pinned `Ed25519Verifier` by value also drops the `self.committed[i]` bounds check on the hot pinned path.

**Worth fixing: yes.** It is ~15 lines, it removes the one term that scales with attacker/owner-controlled commitment size rather than with work done, and it is exactly the class of amplification the PR exists to close. Note this code is unchanged by the diff, but the diff is what makes it the dominant residual cost, and `crates/core/src/seal/section.rs:264-274`'s new doc comment now explicitly reasons about "either side of that sum" — the decompression term is a third side that comment doesn't account for.

---

### 2. `verify_structure` rebuilds the CBOR preimage on every trial — real but negligible, and not worth the architectural cost
`adoption.rs:369-374`, calling `/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box/.claude/worktrees/agent-a3ae17b99e0dc6e1b/crates/core/src/seal/structure.rs:91-99`

Each trial iteration re-runs `structure_sig_preimage(input)`: a `Map` build with 4-5 `Value::Bytes(..to_vec())` heap allocations plus a det-CBOR encode into a fresh `Vec<u8>`. The preimage is **invariant across the whole loop** — only the verifier changes. Worst case that is 1024 redundant encodes and ~5000 redundant small allocations per record.

**Concrete weight:** a ~100-byte CBOR encode plus five allocations is sub-microsecond; 1024 of them is tens of µs against 1024 `verify_strict` calls (hundreds of ms in WASM). **< 0.05%.** The only way to hoist it is to call `pseudonym.verify(&preimage, &sig)` directly in the gate, which moves core's fail-closed `TrustViolation::StructureSignatureInvalid` policy into `adoption.rs` and breaks "the gate composes core's verify functions and invents no cryptographic error code of its own". **Not worth fixing.** (If you ever want it, the right shape is a `verify_structure_preimage(&verifier, &preimage, &sig)` in `structure.rs` that both entry points share — but only alongside a benchmark showing it registers.)

`Ed25519Signature::from_bytes(*signature)` at `:365` is a 64-byte memcpy into a newtype — free, and correctly hoisted above the loop already.

---

### 3. `authenticate_section_structures` closure — clean, nothing retained
`adoption.rs:395-401`

The `authenticate` closure captures `auth` by unique borrow and `scope`/`epoch` by reference to `Copy` locals; no clone of the section, the commitment, or any ciphertext. `auth` (and its `Vec<Ed25519Verifier>`) is a stack local dropped at return, so **no long-lived object holds the 200 KB verifier vector or the section alive** past the call — this passes the "closure keeps a large scope alive" check. `let (scope, epoch) = (envelope.scope, envelope.epoch)` at `:394` is a 24-byte copy done once, not per structure. **No finding.**

---

### 4. `kat_gen.rs` — `commit_grantee` recomputes an identical ECDSA commitment signature four times
`/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box/.claude/worktrees/agent-a3ae17b99e0dc6e1b/crates/engine/examples/kat_gen.rs:357-367`, invoked at `:380`, `:408`, `:420`, `:438`

All four invocations pass the same `&fixture.grant_section` and push the same `GrantSetEntry`, so each does a full `GrantSection::clone()` (deep — every ciphertext `Vec`) and a `sign_grant_set` over **byte-identical** commitment bytes, producing four identical signatures. Three of the four ECDSA signs and one of the four clones are pure waste.

**Cheaper:** build `let committed = commit_grantee(&fixture.grant_section);` once, then `committed.clone()` per variant (saves 3 ECDSA signs; the clones remain necessary since each variant mutates). **Worth fixing: marginal.** ~150 µs in an offline generator run by hand and in CI. The real argument is legibility — it makes "all four vectors share one commitment" structural rather than incidental, which is load-bearing for the accept family's non-vacuity claim at `:355`. `head_block` (`:369`) clones the envelope and re-encodes once per vector, which is required (each vector carries a different section). `owner_identity_pk.clone()` at `:455`/`:469` is 4 small `String` clones — ignore.

---

### 5. `kat_gate.rs::signers_per_structure` — called once per vector per test, not repeatedly; cost is nil
`/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box/.claude/worktrees/agent-a3ae17b99e0dc6e1b/crates/engine/tests/kat_gate.rs:117-183`, called at `:241` and `:275`

Correcting the premise in the brief: `stage_two` is called exactly **once per vector per test** (`:227` path and `:266` path are different tests over disjoint vector files), and `signers_per_structure` once per vector. It does not run repeatedly.

The actual work: 4 vectors total (2 accept, 2 reject), each head block ~570-675 bytes. Per vector, `signers_per_structure` rebuilds the committed verifier list (2 decompressions) and deliberately runs the **full product without early exit** — that is the point, it must report *every* pseudonym each structure verifies under so the test can assert `len() == 1` and `distinct == 2`. With 2 pseudonyms × 3-4 structures that is **6-8 verifies per vector, ~30 verifies across the whole suite**, plus 4 ECDSA `verify_grant_set` in `stage_two`. Total under a millisecond.

`manifest()` (`:75`) re-parses the JSON manifest in each of 4 tests and `vectors()` (`:79`) re-parses a fixture file on each call (twice in `manifest_header_and_counts_are_exact`) — ~3 KB of JSON, single-digit µs. **Not worth fixing**, and both are test-only with a clear readability payoff for the redundancy; the no-early-exit product is required by what the assertions mean, so it is not waste.

---

## Summary

One finding is worth acting on: **#1**, the eager point decompression in `committed_write_pseudonyms`. Everything else is either already correctly placed (#3), negligible with a real architectural cost to fix (#2), or test/generator-only noise (#4, #5). Nothing in the diff introduces blocking work on a hot path, sequential-but-independent operations, or a closure that keeps a large enclosing scope alive.</result>

## Report

**PR #1120** — https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/pull/1120 (draft, branch `fix/pin-adoption-gate-section-signer`, 2 commits, all CI green)

### What I implemented

The gate's stage 3 now **pins the section's signer**: the committed write-capable pseudonym that authenticates the section's first structure is pinned, and every later structure must verify under that key alone. A section signed by two committed pseudonyms is a whole-record `structure-signature-invalid` trust violation.

I verified the vulnerability myself first, and found a second consequence the issue did not name: per-structure trial-verify also adopted a **structure splice** — a structure lifted verbatim from a different record at the same scope and epoch by a different committed writer recomputes an identical signed input, so it verified. That is an integrity hole, not just a CPU one, and it is now the leading argument in the blueprint.

Per the issue's four requirements:
1. **Blueprint** — `blueprint/engine.md` states "one section, one signer" normatively at the gate spec. `blueprint/core.md` and `crates/core/src/seal/section.rs` justified the 1024/256 caps with "one signature per structure per committed pseudonym", which is no longer the shape; both now cross-reference the engine rule. `blueprint/testing.md` records the new suite and its gate.
2. **Rule-8 mirror** — verified, not assumed: `net/author.rs::check_scope_root` already calls the same `authenticate_section_structures`, so symmetry holds by construction. Added a release-active test (returns `Err`, no assert) where both signers are committed and the commitment is re-signed, so only the pin can reject it.
3. **KAT reject vector** — a self-contained engine KAT set under `crates/engine/kat/gate/`, generator-written, consumed by a new `crates/engine/tests/kat_gate.rs`. Two accept + two reject (mixed-signer, structure-splice). Non-vacuity proven: I reverted `adoption.rs` and confirmed both the generator and the suite fail.
4. **Multi-writer answer** — **No**, in the PR body with citations. `CONTEXT.md` and both blueprints all say "the rotator" singular; the commitment names many pseudonyms so **any** write-capable client can be the rotator, not so several can co-sign. Today it's stronger still: `reseal_scope_root` accepts only the owner pseudonym.

### Measured before/after (release, 1025 pseudonyms × 1284 structures)

| case | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| adversarial (signers spread) | 1,316,100 verifications, **74.6 s**, **ADOPTED** | 1,026 verifications, **35 ms**, rejected |
| honest worst case | 2,308 verifications, 80.6 ms | 2,308 verifications, 75.9 ms |

### Gates (all unpiped, exit codes)

`cargo fmt --all --check` 0 · `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0 · `cargo test --workspace` 0 · `cargo check -p cipherbox-wasm --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` 0 · engine `kat_gen` + porcelain 0/clean · core `kat_gen` + diff 0/clean · `pnpm lint:tracker-refs` 0 · markdownlint + prettier 0. Generator determinism verified by diffing two runs.

### Review-gate findings and resolutions

`/security-review`: no findings. `/crypto-privacy-review`: no CRITICAL/HIGH — `verify_strict` rules out the duplicate-signature trick that could steer the pin; the change is a strict narrowing. Two MEDIUM + two LOW, all fixed. `/simplify` (4 agents): fixed and folded into commit 2 —

- **KAT strength** — the reject vector couldn't distinguish "pin fired" from "junk signature", and the accept commitment named one pseudonym so an over-tightening to index 0 would have gone uncaught. All vectors now share a two-pseudonym commitment; the harness proves every reject signature is individually valid and that two signers are named.
- **Efficiency** — `committed_write_pseudonyms` eagerly decompressed up to 1025 Ed25519 points per record though the pin uses at most one: an `O(pseudonyms)` term the pin otherwise removes. Now lazy; honest worst case 81.5 → 75.9 ms.
- **Reuse** — the KAT harness hand-rolled the committed set (**silently dropping the dedup pass**, so it trial-verified a different candidate set than the gate) and the structure walk. Extracted `for_each_structure` as the single definition.
- **Visibility** — my first `#[cfg(feature = "test-kit")]` split was hollow (four crates enable it; Cargo unifies graph-wide). Replaced with the house pattern `#[doc(hidden)] pub`.

**Pushed back on one finding**: the mirror belongs in `net/author.rs`, not `rotation/reseal.rs` — a mixed-signer section is structurally unconstructable there, so the check would guard an impossibility.

### Deliberately out of scope (filed, bidirectional native dependency edges verified)

- **#1131** — move stage 3 into `crates/core` behind a `VerifiedGrantSet` witness. The altitude pass argued the layering is inverted (core's caps are justified by an algorithm core can't see; the stage-2 precondition is prose where it could be a type). Real, but touches core primitives, `verify_grant_set`'s signature and the core KAT manifest. Counter-argument recorded in the issue.
- **#1132** — fold the gate KAT family into the single engine manifest, as core does with fourteen families. Blocked on restructuring `kat_content.rs`, which I don't own.

### Files touched beyond my stated ownership — flagging explicitly

`crates/engine/src/gate/mod.rs` (re-export line), `crates/core/src/seal/section.rs` (one doc comment my change made stale), `.prettierignore` (`crates/engine/kat/` was missing next to `crates/core/kat/` — my generated files would have been prettier-rewritten, failing a gate they can't fix). A device with no projected head resolves one at `beginWrite` before anything is spent. The drain projects the head its own publishes established via `project_child_version`, so a device never reads its own landed publish as a concurrent writer.

That is broken two ways — a queued predecessor and a concurrent writer advance a count identically (so the second of two queued edits published straight over the writer that beat the first: the original bug, reached with two local edits), and `RetentionPolicy::KeepLatest` moves a count backwards. content.content:
Prune drops old file versions and reclaims their bytes. Prune is a **write-plane mutation** — it re-seals and publishes a shortened history — which is why #820 pulled it into this chain. Slice settled by #825 on wayfinder map #813.

## Scope

**This issue absorbs #849, #850 and #851 outright.** They were previously named as prerequisites in prose only, with no dependency edge, which made #872 look startable when it is not — and made three defects look like three shippable PRs. They are not: `plan_prune` (`crates/engine/src/content/retention.rs:93`) has **zero production callers** at `main` @ `3d087d673`. Its only references are the re-exports at `crates/engine/src/lib.rs:54` and `crates/engine/src/content/mod.rs:38`, and its own unit tests in `retention.rs`. Nothing reaches it, so none of the three is independently observable or independently testable end-to-end. Close all three as folded-in when this ships. Native `blocked_by` edges are recorded on this issue so the graph stays honest until they are.

**Three correctness fixes, folded in.**

- **#849 — leaf expansion.** `plan_prune` emits root content CIDs only, and `POST /registry/retire` deletes rows for exactly the CIDs handed to it without walking the DAG, so every sealed leaf stays pinned and charged forever while `reclaimed_bytes` reports the whole version freed. Expand each doomed root to `root + leaf_cids` before retiring, by fetching the root block and `decode_root`-ing it — the root block is plaintext det-CBOR, so no key is needed. Two constraints on its shape: `root + leaf_cids` **cannot be one call** — the registry batch cap is `REGISTRY_BATCH_MAX = 1000` (`crates/engine/src/net/mod.rs:25`), enforced by the chunking at `crates/engine/src/net/retire.rs:100`, and a 1 GiB version is 1025 targets at the frozen 1 MiB framing, so partial retire is normal at exactly `max_file_bytes` — and **leaves retire before their root**.
- **#850 — unit mismatch.** `ContentVersion.size_bytes` (`crates/engine/src/content/retention.rs:75`) is documented as the **pinned** size, but the prune path fills it from `Version.size`, which is **plaintext** bytes. The gap is fixed and computable (40 B per sealed leaf, plus the root block). A pending-reclaim total built on the wrong unit is the same misreport in a new place. Derive the pinned total from the leaf count and root size rather than reusing the plaintext number.
- **#851 — partially already fixed; check before you write.** The ticket claimed `keep_latest` admits zero at `retention.rs:72-73`. That is stale in two ways. `RetentionPolicy::KeepLatest(NonZeroU64)` **already exists** (`crates/engine/src/content/retention.rs:65`), with the doc stating the zero state is unrepresentable rather than guarded. The hole survives only on the free function: `plan_prune(versions_newest_first: &[ContentVersion], keep_latest: usize)` at `retention.rs:93` still takes a plain `usize` and `skip(0)` still yields the whole history including the live version. Close that one signature; do not re-do the enum.

**One op that ends at publish, plus a retire ledger that is not an op** (#852). Both alternatives put a garbage-collection call on the critical path of user work: one op with two legs holds the FIFO head so the next rename waits on cleanup, and two ops repeats that plus a sixth `OpKind` with vacuous rebase semantics.

**The ledger stores roots; leaves are re-derived** at drain time via `decode_root` — plaintext det-CBOR, no key. That is three orders of magnitude smaller, and it is the irrecoverable half: once the publish lands nothing readable references the dropped roots, while leaves always can be recovered from a root.

**Leaves before root, versions oldest-first.** The journaled root **is** the expansion key, so retiring it first makes its leaf list unnameable and those bytes charged forever. Oldest-first is what `plan_prune` already emits — `PrunePlan.retire_targets` is documented "oldest first" (`content/retention.rs:82`) and the plan is built by iterating the doomed suffix in reverse (`content/retention.rs:99-103`) — and it leaves a valid suffix of history. Together these make the drain resumable across restart with nothing journaled but roots.

**Entries clear only on the server's own done-signal** — a batch reporting `retired: 0`, which is positive evidence and also covers the succeeded-but-response-lost case. Everything else backs off forever: **no attempt budget, no gave-up list, no dead-letter class.** Every failure is either self-clearing (offline, 401, a 429 from the registry throttle, a 503 from lock contention) or ours (a 400 from a bad CID we emitted, an unfetchable root we are charging for), and in every case the only user action is `Command::ManualRefresh`, which already exists.

**Owed bytes ride the entry** as one `u64` from `ContentVersion.size_bytes` — in the corrected pinned unit, per the folded-in #850 — and surface as a **vault-level pending-reclaim figure** beside the quota, the ticket's own missing "record of what was owed".

**Mode-derived legs, bytes tracking hosted.** Hosted to hosted, External to provider, Dual to both; the byte figure drains on hosted confirmation. External accounts hold **size-zero rows** (`register()` records membership at size 0, hosted ingress refused for BYO, `content.service.ts:246-253`), so a hosted-only ledger would self-satisfy instantly in External mode.

**A distinct `RetireLedger` seam** with its own conformance kit, on `FloorStore`'s precedent. It diverges from the op queue on lifetime, ordering (a set, not a FIFO), failure contract (never-discard versus dead-letter) and cancellability at once. Reusing the op queue is cheaper and inherits #832's owner tag free, but it puts a non-FIFO non-cancellable record in a store whose cold-start sweep **deletes** what it cannot decode.

**Owner-scoping is forced, not tidy.** Account A's owed CIDs retried under account B's token delete no rows, return `retired: 0`, and satisfy the done-signal without reclaiming anything.

## Harvest reference

`apps/api/src/ipfs/pending-unpin/` on branch `v1` is the same shape server-side: a durable outbox drained in ordered batches, per-row failure isolation ("leave row for next run; do not abort the batch"), a refcount-then-unpin helper, and a depth gauge. v1 could place it server-side only because it called Kubo `pin/ls` directly; v2 cannot, since no endpoint lists an account's pin rows (#826).

## Acceptance

- `plan_prune` cannot be called with a zero keep-count — unrepresentable, not guarded.
- `reclaimed_bytes` equals the sum of the sizes the retire call actually frees, in pinned bytes.
- A pruned 1 GiB version retires across multiple `REGISTRY_BATCH_MAX` batches, leaves before root, and is resumable after a mid-drain restart.
- A retire returning `retired: 0` clears the entry; every other failure retries.
- The pending-reclaim figure drains to zero on hosted confirmation and never on an External-only leg.

## Gate

`Engine Tests`, `Contract Suite`.

(1) The batch cap was cited as `MAX_BATCH = 1000`; that constant lives at `crates/load/src/plan.rs:119` and is an unrelated load-test bound. The real cap is `REGISTRY_BATCH_MAX = 1000` at `crates/engine/src/net/mod.rs:25`, enforced at `crates/engine/src/net/retire.rs:100`. (2) #849/#850/#851 were named as prerequisites in prose with no dependency edge, so this issue read as startable. Since `plan_prune` has no production caller, none of the three is reachable standalone; they are folded into this scope, native `blocked_by` edges added, and they close as folded-in when this ships. (3) #851 was half-refuted: `RetentionPolicy::KeepLatest(NonZeroU64)` already exists at `content/retention.rs:65`; only `plan_prune`'s own `usize` parameter at `:93` still admits zero. The oldest-first cite `content/retention.rs:78-80` was also stale — that is the `PrunePlan` doc header; the behaviour is at `:82` and `:99-103`.

Closes #849, #850, #851

input.command:
cat > /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-myankelev-Code-random-cipher-box/8ed080ed-fffa-498c-9012-8e777bd9ef50/scratchpad/close-1115.md <<'EOF'
Closing unmerged: #849, #850 and #851 are folded into #872 rather than shipped separately.

`plan_prune` has zero production callers, so nothing here is reachable or observable at runtime, and #872 would immediately reshape the expansion around the retire ledger. #872's own body already absorbs all three and carries `Closes #849, #850, #851`, so they close when it ships. That was the recommendation in the audit comments on all three issues; shipping this PR would have landed an expansion with no caller.

**The branch is kept, not deleted** — `fix/prune-leaf-expansion-and-pinned-units` @ `head`. It is a working reference for #872's implementer, and lands in the shapes #872 specifies:

- `expand_retire_targets(version, root_block)` returns leaves first and the root **last**, one level, block-size-capped before hashing. The address check routes through core's `decode_content_cid_str` + `is_plane_anchor` + `verify_cid`, so a mismatch carries the already-KAT-pinned `TrustViolation::ContentCidMismatch`.
- `size_bytes` -> `pinned_bytes` with `ContentVersion::from_plaintext_size(cid, plaintext, profile)` as the explicit conversion, bound at runtime: the expansion refuses unless the manifest's leaf count and root-block length account for exactly the pinned total the plan quoted.
- `plan_prune` takes `NonZeroU64`, matching the `RetentionPolicy::KeepLatest(NonZeroU64)` the call site already holds.

Verified along the way and worth keeping: `registry.service.ts` `retire` needs **no change** — it already advisory-locks every path, bulk-deletes via `In(targets)`, and refcounts before unpinning. It was only ever missing the full target set from the client.

Two findings from this work are filed against #872 and stay open: #1124 (the expansion cannot subtract a leaf a retained version also references — adversarially reachable via a write-grantee) and #1125 (`sync/drain.rs`'s `registry_cids` derives the same CID set with the opposite ordering, and nothing holds the two equal).
EOF

26	
27	1. `gh api --jq --arg h "$HEAD"` — `gh api` takes no `--arg`. The filter errors, the count comes back empty, the verdict is never detected. Interpolate the value into the jq string instead.

Two of three items were fully delivered; the third (a Service Worker killed outright strands its media cursors) is a distinct design problem now tracked in #1097. Lesson: a second-hand "already delivered" claim is a hypothesis, not a fact — verify per acceptance criterion, and ask which named CI gate would go red on a regression.

**Issues filed this session:** #1091 (selection model), #1092 (text editor dialog), #1093 (current-version details panel), #1094 (engine: retain prior versions) / #1095 (web: version history), #1096 (e2e write-path coverage), #1097 (killed-SW cursor reclamation). All `v2-build`, parented, edged.

## Running a review cycle

Use `~/.claude/projects/-Users-myankelev-Code-random-cipher-box/recycle-both.sh <PR> [notbefore-epoch]`. **`review2.sh` and `cycle.sh` are broken — do not use them.**

Rebase every PR onto current `main` before its cycle, and re-verify locally; CI otherwise runs against a base that no longer exists.

**Six defect classes, all found in this machinery in one session, every one failing toward a false all-clear.** Any cycle log predating 2026-08-05 may be reporting "no findings" when nothing was reviewed:

1. `gh api --jq --arg h "$HEAD"` — `gh api` takes no `--arg`. The filter errors, the count comes back empty, the verdict is never detected. Interpolate the value into the jq string instead.
2. Re-drafting on the first CodeRabbit status-comment touch (~1 min) cuts both bots off — macroscope needs ~4-7 min and CodeRabbit ~8.5 min after the flip. Hold ready until both actually land on the head.
3. A **clean** CodeRabbit verdict posts NO review at all — only an edit to its status comment. Polling review bodies alone hangs to timeout on a passing PR. Poll both surfaces and require the comment's `updated_at` to have moved past a pre-flip baseline.
4. "Nothing pending" is trivially true in the window before GitHub registers any check. Require a plausible settled-check count (this repo runs ~23) before believing green.
5. `$GH pr ready $PR >/dev/null && echo FLIPPED` swallows a network failure, then polls a still-draft PR for its full timeout. **Confirm the flip by re-reading `isDraft`, and retry.** Same for the re-draft.
6. A timed-out head fetch yields `HEAD=""`, which silently matches nothing everywhere downstream. Retry and validate 40-hex before proceeding.

**The CodeRabbit fence:** 1/hr org-wide, measured from the last CR review's `submitted_at`. Compute it only from GitHub timestamps — `date -u -j -f "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ" "<submitted_at>" +%s` + 3600 + 90. **Never read a local test runner's clock**: vitest prints `Start at HH:MM:SS` in *local* time, and taking it as UTC once burned a cycle on a rate-limit notice.

## Hard-won rules

- **Verify the COMMITTED tree, never the working tree.** A rebase resolution edited on disk but not committed passed every local gate and pushed the broken commit anyway. Use `git show HEAD:<path>`; require `git status --porcelain` empty *before and after* the gates.
- **Two PRs adding the same field to one interface merge CLEAN into a duplicate.** #1071 and #1081 both added `folder: Uint8Array | null` to `useFolderNavigation.ts` at different offsets: git stopped on `FileBrowser.tsx` (visible) but silently doubled the field (`TS2300` ×2, `TS1117`). `mergeable=CLEAN` proves nothing. Simulate with `git merge-file -p <ours> <base> <theirs>` and grep for a doubled declaration *before* the second PR merges. See [[project-semantic-merge-conflict-shape-change]].
- **Don't let a loose success check stand in for a read-back.** Reporting "parented"/"blocked_by" from a substring match on the API response was wrong in one direction and right in the other; only re-reading the authoritative list caught it. Same class as the six defects above.
- **A reviewer's premise can be wrong, not just its fix.** Three findings on #1078 assumed no upload UI existed; it does. Tracked in #1096.
- CodeRabbit **withdrew** two findings on re-review after being pushed back on with mechanism evidence. Pushing back is worth it; see [[feedback-never-apply-review-suggestions-literally]].
- Resolve agents share the primary checkout unless told otherwise — one left it on a feature branch. Brief them to work in a worktree created from `origin/<branch>` (not local HEAD) and to leave the primary tree on `main`.

  OK=$($GH pr view $PR --json statusCheckRollup --jq '[.statusCheckRollup[]|select(.conclusion=="SUCCESS")]|length' 2>/dev/null)
  DONE=$($GH pr view $PR --json statusCheckRollup --jq '[.statusCheckRollup[]|select(.conclusion!=null)]|length' 2>/dev/null)
  echo "[$(date -u +%H:%M:%SZ)] ci: success=$OK settled=$DONE pending=$PEND failed=$FAIL (need >=$MINCHECKS)"

content.text:
Yes, though the value is narrower than "making progress" — it's specifically about the one resource that's serialized.

The review queue is the long pole: five PRs at one slot an hour is ~5 hours minimum, and that cost is unavoidable whenever we pay it. CI isn't a long pole — once Actions recovers, all five run in parallel. Findings are also fixable right now, since the Rust gates all run locally.

content.text:
**#1119 — 3 nitpicks, all three worth taking**, fixed in `1327e2c90` (push retrying, local network is flaky).

The one that mattered most was the **symmetry gap in `revoke_invite_link`**. Its doc comment claims *"a tag that is merely committed belongs to some grantee and is not this function's to cut"* — but the code only checked the tag was present in the commitment. It never confirmed the tag re-derives from the owner's secret and that record's own ephemeral key, which `convert_invite_claim` does at `:529`. So the stated rule wasn't enforced, and an owner-side record mix-up could cut an ordinary grantee's entry.

CodeRabbit rated it defense-in-depth. I'd put it slightly higher: a doc comment asserting an invariant the code doesn't check is how the *next* change reasons wrongly.

**I proved the new check bites rather than trusting it.** The existing `unknown.link` test passes through the commitment lookup, so it says nothing about the re-derivation. I added the case that isolates it — a record carrying another grantee's *committed* tag with its own ephemeral key — then deleted the check and confirmed that assertion goes red, and restored it green. Without that, I'd have shipped a check no test exercises.

The other two: a test for the ambiguous-link refusal (two records sharing one ephemeral identity must refuse, not resolve to first match), and a vacuity guard on the transport leak scan — `windows()` yields nothing when the payload is shorter than the needle, so all three "no plaintext in the clear" assertions could pass without scanning anything. That's the false-all-clear shape that's bitten this repo repeatedly.

Full gates green: fmt, clippy `-D warnings`, the whole engine suite, and the wasm32 target check.

**Two left: #1122, then #1117.**

content.text:
**All seven PRs are now reviewed.** #1117's finding was the best catch of the wave.

`requestPorts()` runs at script evaluation — not an event — with its promise discarded. The browser can stop the worker once the dispatching event settles, so **a worker restarted by a fetch, which is the common case for this exact bug, could die before `clients.matchAll()` and the messaging finished.** The recovery would have looked wired up and silently not run, leaving the predecessor's cursors pinned — precisely what #1097 exists to prevent.

Fixed by retaining the promise and extending the triggering fetch over it. Mutation-checked: deleting only that line leaves the new test as the sole failure (`1 failed | 385 passed`), restoring gives 386.

## Wave 6 review summary

| PR | Verdict | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| #1118 | clean | **merged** |
| #1116 | 1 nitpick | real asymmetry documented at its decision site |
| #1120 | 1 actionable | garbled KAT rationale fixed |
| #1123 | 2 actionable | unbounded test loop + misleading data-loss text |
| #1119 | 3 nitpicks | doc/code mismatch closed, 2 vacuous-test gaps |
| #1122 | 2 actionable | partial-batch retry re-dispatching accepted nodes |
| #1117 | 1 actionable | recovery cut short by worker termination |

Ten findings across six PRs, every one fixed and every thread resolved. Worth noting the pattern: **three of them were tests or checks that couldn't fail** — a vacuous leak scan, a check with no test exercising it, an unbounded loop that hangs instead of asserting. That's the same false-all-clear class that's bitten this repo repeatedly, and it's the strongest argument for having run CodeRabbit over these despite the outage.

Fixed and pushed (`51f23e6a7`), with every gate verified **unpiped** this time: `typecheck=0`, `lint=0`, `build=0`, client tests 386 passing.

**That failure was mine, and worth naming.** I claimed `FetchEventLike` already declared `waitUntil` — it didn't; line 42's optional `waitUntil?` belongs to `PortMessageEventLike`. My local typecheck reported 0 because I piped it through `tail`, so `$?` was `tail`'s exit code. That is exactly the trap I put in the brief for all eight wave-6 agents, and I walked into it myself while verifying someone else's work. CI caught it; my local check was worthless.

The fix is one line — declaring `waitUntil?` on `FetchEventLike` — and the underlying finding stands.

## #1123's semantic conflict: worse than a broken test

The delegated investigation proved it causally rather than by inspection, instrumenting both configurations:

- with #1123's `project_child_version` in `publish_new_file`: `before=(Some(200), Some(0))`, `after=(Some(200), Some(0))` → **silent**
- with that one call disabled (i.e. `main`): `before=(None, None)`, `after=(Some(200), Some(0))` → fires

So **on `main` the test passed because the projection was incomplete, not because the kernel was stale.** On a freshly-minted inode the kernel holds nothing, so that repaint was spurious to begin with.

And the false negative already existed on `main` for local *edits* — `publish_update_content` set `mtime`/`size` inline, silencing the same detector. #1123 merely extended the shape to creates and knocked over the test that had been passing incidentally.

The fix keys the repaint to **what the mount actually served** (`Engine::stream_version_cid`), which is the only thing the kernel's pages can have come from, rather than to a projection delta that is neither necessary nor sufficient evidence about the kernel. Both replacement tests were mutation-checked.

I tightened one thing after review: `engine_mut` was public API with only a test caller, now `#[doc(hidden)]` per the `crates/core/src/kdf` precedent.

Current CI: #1120 24 green, #1119 19 green, #1122 20 green; #1123 and #1117 rerunning on their new heads. #1116 still needs its re-trigger, which I'll do once these settle.

skills.name: resolve-pr-reviews
skills.content:
# Resolve PR Review Comments

Resolve all open review comments on the current PR from any automated reviewer (CodeRabbit, GitHub Copilot, etc.) or human reviewers.

## Workflow

### 1. Identify the PR

```bash
PR_NUMBER=$(gh pr view --json number --jq '.number')
```

If no PR exists for the current branch, stop and inform the user.

### 2. Fetch all unresolved review threads

Use the GraphQL `reviewThreads` query to get threads with `isResolved` status:

```bash
REPO_OWNER=$(gh repo view --json owner --jq '.owner.login')
REPO_NAME=$(gh repo view --json name --jq '.name')

gh api graphql -f query="
{
  repository(owner: \"$REPO_OWNER\", name: \"$REPO_NAME\") {
    pullRequest(number: $PR_NUMBER) {
      reviewThreads(first: 100) {
        nodes {
          id
          isResolved
          comments(first: 10) {
            nodes {
              id
              author { login }
              body
              path
              line
              createdAt
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}"
```

Filter to only unresolved threads. If none, report "No unresolved review threads" and stop.

### 3. Triage each comment

For each unresolved thread, read the comment and the referenced code. Categorize as:

- **Valid fix needed** — the comment identifies a real bug, security issue, or meaningful improvement
- **Already addressed** — the issue was fixed in a later commit on this branch
- **Not applicable** — the suggestion doesn't apply (explain why)

### 4. Implement fixes

For all "valid fix needed" comments:

1. Read the referenced file and understand the context
2. Implement the fix
3. Track which thread the fix addresses

Do NOT:

- Make unrelated changes or refactors
- Add features beyond what the comment requests
- Increase timeouts or add retries as a first approach — fix root causes

### 5. Run tests locally

After ALL fixes are implemented:

```bash
# Type check
pnpm typecheck

# Run relevant unit tests
pnpm test

# If E2E-relevant changes were made, run E2E tests too
cd tests/web-e2e && pnpm exec playwright test
```

Do NOT proceed to commit until tests pass. If tests fail, fix the failures first.

### 6. Commit and push

```bash
git add <specific-files>
git commit -m "fix: address PR review comments"
git push
```

### 7. Reply to and resolve each thread

For each thread, reply explaining what was done, then resolve:

- **Fixed comments**: Reply with what was changed and where, then resolve
- **Already addressed**: Reply explaining which commit addressed it, then resolve
- **Not applicable**: Reply with clear reasoning for not making changes, then resolve

Reply via REST (use `--field` not `-f` for `in_reply_to` — must be integer):

```bash
gh api repos/$REPO_OWNER/$REPO_NAME/pulls/$PR_NUMBER/comments \
  --field in_reply_to=COMMENT_ID \
  --raw-field body='...'
```

Resolve via GraphQL (can batch multiple):

```bash
gh api graphql -f query='
mutation {
  resolveReviewThread(input: {threadId: "THREAD_ID"}) {
    thread { isResolved }
  }
}'
```

### 8. Report summary

Print a summary table:

- Thread count resolved
- Fixes made (with file:line references)
- Comments marked as already addressed or not applicable

content.text:
Yes — three of them. I checked each PR's CR review commit against the branch tip, so this is the diff CodeRabbit has never seen:

| PR | Unreviewed since CR | What changed | Re-review? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **#1119** | `1327e2c90` | `crates/engine/src/grants/invite.rs` +38 — new tag re-derivation guard in `revoke_invite_link` | **Yes — crypto** |
| **#1123** | `8a44f9a43`, `aca8f1726` | `crates/fuse/src/ops.rs` +48/-29, `facade.rs` +11 (new `stream_version_cid`), tests +82 | **Yes** |
| **#1122** | `1dd570730` | `useVaultActions.ts` +77, `FileBrowserActions.tsx` +57 — `move`/`remove` return type changed | **Yes** |
| #1120 | — | CR re-reviewed at `558149e70`; current tip is that content rebased | No |
| #1117 | `51f23e6a7` | 2 lines: `waitUntil?` added to `FetchEventLike` | No |

The three that qualify all changed **behavior after the verdict**, not just prose:

- **#1119** is the strongest case. The fix adds a fail-closed check on the revoke path — re-deriving the record's tag so a record from another scope root can't cut an ordinary grantee's entry. It's a new crypto invariant in a trust boundary, and AGENTS.md makes `/crypto-privacy-review` mandatory for exactly this. CR reviewed the PR *without* that guard existing.
- **#1123** is the semantic-conflict repair, not a CR finding at all — it replaced the projection-delta staleness detector with one keyed to `Engine::stream_version_cid`, and exposed new engine surface to do it. That's the largest unreviewed behavior delta in the wave.
- **#1122** changed a public hook contract: `move`/`remove` went from `Promise<boolean>` to `Promise<BatchOutcome>`, with a new `runBatch` that sets `busy`/`error` outside the `try/finally` that `run` uses. Benign as written (every dispatch is caught), but it's a second, divergent state-management path CR never saw.

#1117's post-review commit is the type declaration that fixed the `TS2339` CI break — no runtime change; the substantive `waitUntil` fix at `055ed62a5` *was* reviewed.

**Recommendation:** spend re-review slots on #1119 and #1123, merge #1120, #1122, #1117 on a straight flip-to-ready. I'd drop #1122 from the re-review list despite the table — it's UI-layer, has new unit tests covering the batch outcomes, and at one slot per hour it's not worth two hours of the queue against a hook signature change. If you'd rather not spend any slots, #1119 is the one I'd not skip.

Confirmed — both threads on #1123 are resolved with CodeRabbit explicitly agreeing to my alternatives (the `baseSuperseded` wording and the counter-plus-assert drain bound), including agreeing that a "reopen and save again" hint would be wrong until there's a recover surface.

To be straight about what that does and doesn't settle: those threads were findings against `9c8f19323`, and CR re-reviewed at that commit. My concern was the *later* pair — `8a44f9a43` (the `stream_version_cid` repaint fix) and `aca8f1726` — which CR has never seen. Thread acceptance doesn't cover them.

What does change my recommendation is the slot economics you've just made explicit. Flipping #1123 ready fires a CR review either way, so "merge without re-review" doesn't save a slot — it saves an hour of wall clock. The trade is one hour for a review pass on that FUSE commit.

**Merge it now — don't wait.** Two reasons:

1. **CR's demonstrated yield on this PR was two Minor maintainability notes** — loop bounding and UI copy. Zero correctness catches. It reviewed the pre-fix `ops.rs` and did not flag the projection gap that turned into the #1118 semantic conflict. The class of defect sitting in the unreviewed commit is precisely the class CR structurally doesn't catch: cross-PR interaction, invisible in a single-PR diff.
2. **That commit is the best-covered change in the wave.** `fuse_op_core.rs` gained 82 lines, and I confirmed the coverage fires in both directions by instrumentation — broken version fails, fixed version passes. It's not resting on review to be correct.

The honest counterweight: it's still the largest unreviewed behavior delta in wave 6, and its failure mode is a stale read served from a mount. I'd weigh that differently if it were unreviewed *and* untested, or if it touched crypto — it's neither.

Say the word and I'll flip #1123 ready. Then I'd spend the next slot on **#1122** rather than banking it: its unreviewed commit changed a public hook contract (`move`/`remove` from `Promise<boolean>` to `Promise<BatchOutcome>`) and added a second state-management path alongside `run`, which is the kind of shape CR is genuinely good at.

---
name: ASD-STE100
description: Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100) for prose. Code, identifiers, paths, and quoted output pass through unchanged.
---

Write all prose in Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100). The specification
is the authority. This file gives the rules and a working subset of the
dictionary; when the two disagree, obey the specification.

## What this applies to

Apply STE to prose: explanations, reports, recommendations, questions, and
summaries.

Do **not** apply STE to these. Give them unchanged:

- Code, in a block or inline.
- File paths, identifiers, commands, flags, and branch names.
- Quoted output: errors, logs, test results, diffs, tool results.
- Text that a standard controls: commit messages (Conventional Commits), PR
  titles, and the code comments of a repository.

Do not repair the grammar of quoted material. Quote it exactly.

## Words

1. Use a word from the approved dictionary, a technical name, or a technical
   verb. Use no other word.
2. One word has one meaning. One meaning has one word. Do not use two words for
   one thing in the same reply.
3. Use a word in one part of speech only. `check` is a verb; for the noun, write
   `the check`  only if the tool is named that.
4. Do not use contractions. Write `do not`, not `don't`.
5. Do not use a word that shows feeling about the work: `unfortunately`,
   `obviously`, `simply`, `just`, `clearly`, `of course`, `nicely`, `elegant`.
6. Do not use an idiom or a metaphor. Write what occurs.

### Technical names

A technical name is a noun that names a thing in the domain. Technical names are
approved. Use them.

For software work, these are technical names: `commit`, `branch`, `merge`,
`rebase`, `repository`, `function`, `type`, `test`, `gate`, `worktree`. Use the
name that the repository uses. If the repository has a vocabulary document (for
example `CONTEXT.md`), that document is the list of approved technical names.
Use those terms exactly.

### Technical verbs

If no approved verb names the action, use the verb of the domain: `commit`,
`merge`, `rebase`, `push`, `compile`, `deploy`. Use one such verb for one
action, always the same one.

### Approved words for common unapproved ones

| Write         | Do not write                                            |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| about         | approximately, regarding, concerning, with respect to    |
| after         | subsequent to, following                                 |
| also          | in addition, furthermore, moreover                       |
| because       | due to the fact that, owing to, since (for a cause)      |
| before        | prior to, in advance of                                  |
| but           | however, nevertheless, nonetheless                       |
| can           | is able to, is capable of                                |
| change        | modify, alter, amend, revise                             |
| check         | verify, validate, confirm                                |
| do            | perform, carry out, execute, conduct                     |
| enough        | sufficient, adequate                                     |
| find          | locate, ascertain, determine                             |
| get           | obtain, acquire                                          |
| give, supply  | provide, furnish                                         |
| help          | assist, aid, facilitate                                  |
| if            | in the event that, in case                               |
| keep          | retain, preserve, maintain                               |
| let           | allow, permit, enable                                    |
| make sure     | ensure                                                   |
| many          | numerous, a large number of                              |
| more          | additional, further                                      |
| must          | shall, is required to                                    |
| must not      | shall not, is prohibited from                            |
| need          | require, necessitate                                     |
| now           | at this time, currently, presently                       |
| only          | solely, exclusively, merely                              |
| part          | component, element, portion                              |
| problem       | issue, concern                                           |
| put           | place, position (as a verb)                              |
| same          | identical, equivalent                                    |
| see           | refer to, consult                                        |
| show          | indicate, demonstrate, illustrate, display (as a verb)   |
| so            | thus, therefore, hence, consequently                     |
| start         | commence, initiate, begin                                |
| stop          | cease, terminate, discontinue, halt                      |
| tell          | inform, notify, advise                                   |
| then          | subsequently, thereafter                                 |
| try to        | attempt to, endeavor to                                  |
| use           | utilize, employ, leverage                                |
| with          | by means of, via                                         |

## Verbs

7. Use the active voice. Write `I ran the tests`, not `the tests were run`.
8. Use these verb forms only: the infinitive, the imperative, the simple
   present, the simple past, the simple future.
9. Do not use a perfect tense. Write `I pushed the branch`, not `I have pushed
   the branch`.
10. Do not use a progressive tense and do not use an `-ing` word. Write `I run
    the gates now`, not `I am running the gates`.
11. A past participle can be an adjective: `the failed test` is correct. A
    present participle cannot: write `the test that fails`, not `the failing
    test`.
12. Do not turn a verb into a noun. Write `I rebased the branch`, not `I did a
    rebase of the branch`.

## Sentences

13. A sentence in a procedure has 20 words or fewer.
14. A sentence in descriptive text has 25 words or fewer.
15. A paragraph in descriptive text has 6 sentences or fewer.
16. One sentence gives one idea. Split a long sentence. Do not join two ideas
    with a semicolon or a dash.
17. Keep the articles `a`, `an`, and `the`. Keep `that` and `which`. Do not
    remove words to make the text shorter.
18. A noun cluster has 3 words or fewer. Write `the cache of the kernel data`,
    not `the kernel data cache repaint key`.
19. Put the words in the usual order: subject, verb, object.

## Procedures

20. Give one instruction in one sentence.
21. Start an instruction with the verb: `Run the gates.` `Rebase the branch.`
22. Put more than two conditions or steps in a vertical list.
23. Give the steps in the order of the work.

## Descriptive text

24. Say what is true. Do not say what is not there and do not say what did not
    occur, unless the user asked.
25. Give the cause before the effect.
26. Use the same term for one thing in the whole reply.

## Warnings and cautions

27. Put a warning before the step it applies to, not after.
28. Start a warning with a command or with the condition. Write `Do not push to
    main.` or `If the gate fails, stop.`
29. Give the risk in one sentence.

## Examples

Not STE:

> I've gone ahead and rebased #1119 onto main — it was a trivial rebase since it
> only touches three files, none of which overlap anything that's landed, so
> there weren't any conflicts to worry about. Currently running the gates.

STE:

> I rebased #1119 onto main. The branch changes 3 files. No file is also changed
> by a merged branch, so the rebase had no conflict. I run the gates now.

Not STE:

> Unfortunately the failing test was caused by a stale projection, which is why
> simply bumping the timeout wouldn't have helped here.

STE:

> A stale projection caused the test to fail. A longer timeout does not correct
> a stale projection.

## Limits of this file

The approved dictionary has about 900 words. The table above gives only the
words that occur most in this work. If you are not sure that a word is approved,
use a shorter and more common word.

content.text:
Created at `~/.claude/output-styles/asd-ste100.md`. Activate it with **`/config`** → Output style → ASD-STE100. It applies to every project, and takes effect on the next message after you select it.

**What it encodes**

The Part 1 writing rules — approved-words-only, one word/one meaning/one part of speech, active voice, restricted verb forms, no `-ing`, no perfect tenses, articles kept, noun clusters ≤ 3, sentences ≤ 20 words (procedural) / ≤ 25 (descriptive), paragraphs ≤ 6 sentences, one instruction per sentence, warnings before the step.

**Two adaptations you should know about, because STE doesn't cover this domain**

1. **Technical names and technical verbs carry the software vocabulary.** The dictionary is aerospace-maintenance-centric — `commit`, `rebase`, `worktree`, `type` are all absent. STE's own escape hatch is that domain nouns are technical names and domain verbs are admitted when no approved verb fits. The style declares software terms as such, and says that a repo's vocabulary document is the authoritative technical-name list. For cipher-box that means `CONTEXT.md` — which is already a controlled vocabulary, so the fit is unusually good.

2. **A pass-through list.** Code, paths, identifiers, and quoted output (errors, logs, diffs, test results) are exempt, with an explicit instruction not to repair the grammar of quoted material. Commit messages and PR titles are also exempt so STE cannot fight Conventional Commits or your commitlint rule.

**One honest limit**

The approved dictionary is ~900 words and is copyrighted — I can't reproduce it, and I won't pretend the 40-row substitution table is it. The table covers the high-frequency cases in this work; the file says so and tells the model to fall back to shorter, commoner words when unsure. If you want real fidelity, request the spec PDF free for non-commercial use from asd-ste100.org and I can expand the table from it.

**What it will cost you**

STE prose is flatter than what you've been getting. The rules that bite hardest here are no `-ing` and one-idea-per-sentence — a lot of my trade-off explanations ("merge now, because CR's yield on this PR was two Minor notes and the unreviewed commit is well covered") become three short sentences. Judgment survives; the compression doesn't. Your profile says terse-direct, so that may read as an improvement, but be aware STE explicitly forbids dropping articles, so it is *plainer*, not *shorter*.

Wave 6 is unaffected — **#1122** is next, still needing its rebase onto `2ec86e565` once you're ready.
